Their write-up also rates a flaw on an isolated test server as critical and lists twenty low-rated flaws on office laptops. The team can fix only one set this week. Which should it choose?
options: The single flaw the testers rated as critical
The flaws the testers linked in their attack
The twenty low-rated flaws on the office laptops
The flaws that would be quickest to fix
explanation: Reviewing a penetration test report means reading the findings in context, not just by their individual ratings. The three medium findings were shown to work together against production and reach the highest privilege, so breaking any link in that chain removes a proven path to the domain. The critical flaw on an isolated test server matters less here, and fixing the twenty low-rated flaws or the quickest ones first improves the count rather than the risk.

question: A web server's access log shows the request GET /view?page=../../../../etc/passwd answered with status 200. Which attack does this log entry indicate?
explanation: Directory traversal uses ../ sequences to climb out of the folder an application is meant to serve and reach files elsewhere on the server, here the account list in /etc/passwd. Command injection would add a shell command after a separator such as a semicolon. Cross-site scripting would show script or markup in the input, and cross-site request forgery would look like an ordinary request that the user never meant to send.

question: Developers want a copy of the production customer database for testing. Every field must keep its usual format so the tests run normally, and no value in the copy may be reversible to real customer data, even by a lookup the company keeps. Which method fits?
explanation: Static data masking replaces sensitive values in a copy with fictitious values of the same format and keeps no mapping back to the originals, so the change cannot be reversed and the copy is safe for testing. Transparent data encryption protects database files at rest but shows real values to anyone who can query them, tokenization keeps a vault that maps each token back to the real value, and hashing cannot be reversed but turns each value into a digest that no longer looks like a name or number.

question: On a compromised server, the antivirus software and the task list show nothing unusual. A scan run from separate boot media finds a malicious driver that removes its own files and processes from every list the operating system returns. Which type of malware is this?
explanation: A rootkit runs with the operating system's own privileges and hides its files and processes from that system's tools, so it is usually found only by scanning from outside the running system. A Trojan is a harmful program disguised as a useful one. A virus attaches its code to other files and spreads when they are run. A worm spreads across a network by itself.

question: A scanner shows a finding's CVSS vector as CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:L/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H. Which conditions do its AV, PR and UI values describe?
options: Network access, low privileges and required user interaction
Local access, no privileges and required user interaction
Local access, low privileges and no user interaction
Network access, no privileges and no user interaction
explanation: In a CVSS vector, AV:N means the attack vector is the network, PR:L means the attacker needs low privileges, such as an ordinary user account, and UI:R means a user must take some action, such as opening a link, for the attack to work. No privileges would show as PR:N, no user interaction as UI:N and local access as AV:L, and this vector contains none of those values.

question: Logs show that an account limited to HR applications ran a script on its own workstation and, one minute later, held local administrator rights that nobody had assigned to it. No other system was accessed. Which activity does this indicate?
explanation: Privilege escalation is an account gaining rights above those it was given, such as a standard user becoming an administrator. Lateral movement would show the account reaching other systems, and none was accessed. Network reconnaissance would show probing of many hosts or ports. Credential harvesting would show passwords or hashes being collected, for example from memory or from a false login page.

question: A trading platform runs in two data centers at once, each carrying half the load and able to take all of it automatically. A third building has power, cooling and network links but no servers. What are the platform design and the third building?
explanation: Two sites that both carry live traffic and can each take the whole load form an active-active design, and a building with only power, cooling and network links is a cold site. An active-passive design keeps one side idle until a failure, and a warm site is already partly equipped, so it needs less work than a cold site before it can run production.

question: While cleaning up after a malware outbreak, the IT team puts four measures in place. Which of them is a detective control?
options: Re-imaging infected hosts from a known-good baseline image
Application allow listing on each workstation
A login banner warning that systems are monitored
File integrity monitoring that alerts on changed system files
explanation: A detective control identifies and records an attack or a change, and file integrity monitoring does this by alerting when protected system files are altered. Re-imaging infected hosts is corrective, because it restores them after the outbreak, application allow listing is preventive, because it stops unapproved programs from running, and a monitoring banner is a deterrent.

question: An attacker used stolen credentials to move from a compromised workstation to several servers on the same network. Which pair of log sources would BEST reveal this movement?
options: Web server access logs and vulnerability scan reports
Server logon events and internal network flow records
Email security gateway logs and DNS query logs
Perimeter firewall logs and external network flow records
explanation: Lateral movement stays inside the network, so it shows up in the logon events of the servers reached with the stolen account and in internal flow records of the connections between hosts. Perimeter firewall logs and external flow records see only traffic that crosses the internet boundary, web server logs and vulnerability scans show requests to websites and weaknesses, and email gateway and DNS logs show message delivery and name lookups.

question: A network is designed so that every user and device is authenticated and authorized for each connection, no access is granted because of where a request originates, and internal traffic is inspected like external traffic. Which approach to network security does this describe?
explanation: Zero trust assumes that no user, device or location is safe by default, so every request is authenticated, authorized and inspected wherever it comes from. Perimeter security inspects traffic at the network edge and trusts whatever is already inside, defense in depth layers several independent controls, and an air gap physically separates a network from all others.

question: What distinguishes a continuous risk assessment from a recurring one?
options: It starts when a specific event occurs
It repeats on a fixed calendar schedule
It covers a single project and then ends
It updates whenever new data comes in
explanation: A continuous risk assessment runs all the time, usually through automated tools such as scanners and a SIEM, so its results change as soon as new data arrives. A fixed calendar schedule marks a recurring assessment, a start prompted by a specific event marks an ad hoc one, and coverage of a single project that then ends marks a one-time assessment.

question: During a red team exercise, USB drives marked with the word payroll are left in the parking lot, and many employees plug them into their work computers. Which social engineering technique does this exercise test?
explanation: Baiting leaves something tempting, such as a USB drive marked payroll, where people will find it, and counts on curiosity to get the device plugged in and its malware run. Pretexting invents a story to persuade someone, tailgating follows an authorized person through a secured door, and impersonation poses as a specific trusted person or role.

question: A team is choosing between a tabletop exercise and a full failover test. What is the main advantage of the tabletop exercise?
options: It measures how long recovering the system actually takes
It finds gaps in the plan without touching systems
It proves that backups can be read back
It shows that the recovery site can carry live work
explanation: A tabletop exercise talks a scenario through around a table, which exposes gaps in the plan and in people's grasp of their roles at little cost and without touching any system. Measuring how long recovery actually takes needs a failover test, showing that the recovery site can carry live work needs a parallel processing test, and proving that backups can be read back needs a test restore.

question: A company moves its CISO from reporting to the CIO to reporting to the board's risk committee. What does this change mainly achieve?
options: Closer alignment with day-to-day IT projects
Independence from the IT operations it oversees
A sharper focus on legal and regulatory obligations
Tighter control of security spending by finance
explanation: Moving the CISO's reporting line away from the CIO keeps security oversight independent of the IT operations it judges, so risks reach the board without being filtered by the people who run those systems. Reporting to the CIO brings closer alignment with IT projects, reporting to the CFO ties security spending to finance, and reporting to general counsel sharpens the focus on legal and regulatory duties.

question: An outside firm administers a clinic's servers and firewalls under contract. Attackers steal one of that firm's technician accounts and use its remote management tool to install ransomware at the clinic. Which supply chain source was the attackers' way in?
explanation: A firm that runs a customer's systems under contract is a service provider, and its remote access makes it a route into every customer it manages. A hardware provider supplies physical equipment, which was not involved. A software provider writes the programs a customer installs, and the management tool here was abused with a stolen account and was not altered. An identity provider is the system that signs users in.

question: A malware sample creates a scheduled task named WindowsUpdateService. Every 60 seconds it sends a few bytes to one outside address on port 443, and it carries out any commands that come back. Which type of malware is this?
explanation: A remote access Trojan gives an attacker control of a computer: it checks in with its server at regular intervals, a pattern called beaconing, and runs the commands it receives. The scheduled task with a trusted-sounding name only keeps it running after a restart. A logic bomb waits for a set condition and then runs one payload instead of taking orders. A keylogger records keystrokes and sends them out but does not take commands. A worm copies itself to other computers by exploiting them.

question: A bank runs workloads in its own data center, in a private cloud at a colocation site and with a public cloud provider. Compared with using only its own data center, which security challenge does this hybrid design add?
options: Patching thousands of devices in the field
Applying one policy across different platforms
Isolating workloads on a shared host kernel
explanation: A hybrid design spreads workloads over platforms with their own firewalls, logs and policy tools, so applying one security policy across all of them becomes the main added challenge. Patching thousands of devices in the field is the burden of edge computing, isolating workloads on a shared host kernel is the concern of containers, and authenticating calls between small services is the concern of microservices.

question: An attacker unplugs the desktop from a conference room wall port, leaves it disconnected, connects a laptop and sets it to use the desktop's MAC address. Which switch port control would have kept the laptop off the network?
explanation: 802.1X keeps a switch port closed to everything except authentication traffic until the device proves its identity with valid credentials or a certificate, so a copied MAC address gains the attacker nothing. MAC-based port security, even with the desktop's address made sticky on the port, admits any device that presents that address, 802.1Q tagging labels frames with their VLAN on trunk links, and DHCP snooping blocks rogue DHCP servers rather than unauthorized clients.

question: A vendor collected a company's old hard drives and shredded them off site. An auditor now asks for evidence that each drive, listed by serial number, was shredded. Which document should the company provide?
explanation: A certificate of destruction is the vendor's signed statement that named media, often listed by serial number, was destroyed, and it gives the company evidence for its auditors. Chain of custody documents show who held the drives and when, the sanitization policy sets how media must be handled, and the service contract states what the vendor promised, but none of them shows that the shredding was done.

question: Several employees report the same email. The security team confirms that its link opens a fake sign-in page, and that two employees typed their passwords into it. What should the team do FIRST for those two employees?
options: Enroll them in a short course on spotting phishing
Reset their credentials and end their open sessions
Delete the reported email from their inboxes
Scan their laptops and remove any malware found
explanation: Once a user has typed a password into a phishing page, the attacker may already hold it, so the first step for that user is to reset those credentials. A course on spotting phishing is follow-up training rather than containment, a malware scan fits a message that delivered a file, and deleting the email from inboxes is cleanup that does not undo the stolen password.

question: A vendor has just released an emergency patch for a critical flaw, and the security team must find every server that has not yet applied it. Which data source identifies these servers?
explanation: A vulnerability scan checks hosts for known flaws and missing patches, so a scan updated for the new advisory lists every server that still lacks the fix. Intrusion detection alerts show attempts to exploit a flaw rather than which hosts have it, firewall connection logs show allowed and blocked traffic, and NetFlow records show who talked to whom and how much.

question: An insurer will use an AI model to flag claims for fraud review. Which step BEST reduces the risk that the model treats some customers unfairly?
options: Remove age and gender fields from the records the model learns from
Test its error rates across groups and correct any skew found
Confirm that the model's overall accuracy is high on past claims
Encrypt the training data while it is stored, in use and backed up
explanation: Bias is caught by testing outcomes: compare how often, and how wrongly, the model flags each group of customers, and correct unrepresentative or skewed training data, before launch and while the model runs. Removing age and gender leaves proxies such as postal code in place and makes unfairness harder to measure, encryption protects the data's confidentiality rather than its fairness, and high overall accuracy can hide a much higher error rate for one group.

question: A hospital's records system stores a random reference value in place of each patient's national identification number. A separate, tightly controlled service holds the table that returns the real number to authorized processes. Which method of securing data is this?
explanation: Tokenization replaces a sensitive value with a random token and keeps the link between the two in a protected vault, so the token reveals nothing by itself. Encryption produces ciphertext that a key can turn back, hashing produces a one-way digest that cannot be reversed, and masking hides part of a value, as when a card number shows its last four digits alone.

question: A public web server must complete thousands of TLS handshakes each second. Its engineer chooses an elliptic curve (ECDSA P-256) certificate instead of an RSA certificate of comparable security. Which property of elliptic curve cryptography justifies this choice?
options: A fixed-length digest for any input
Shorter keys for a given strength
Fast bulk encryption of large files
explanation: Elliptic curve algorithms reach a given security strength with far shorter keys than RSA (a 256-bit curve is comparable to 3072-bit RSA), so each handshake costs the server less processing. Fast bulk encryption is the role of symmetric ciphers such as AES, and a fixed-length digest is what a hash function produces. Neither RSA nor elliptic curves resist a large quantum computer.

question: Late on a Friday, an administrator learns that attackers are actively exploiting a flaw in the company's production web server software. A vendor patch is available, and the change advisory board next meets on Monday. Under a typical change management policy, how should the patch be handled?
options: As a normal change that is reviewed and scheduled by the board
As an emergency change that is documented and reviewed afterward
As a standard change that is pre-approved and recorded
As a major change that is planned and approved by executives
explanation: An emergency change is applied at once under expedited authorization and is then documented and reviewed by the board after the fact, so urgent risk is handled without giving up accountability. A standard change is a routine, low-risk task that was approved in advance, which an urgent patch to a production server is not. A normal change waits for the board, which would leave the server exposed until Monday. A major change is a high-impact project that needs senior approval and long planning.

question: A company sends the logs from its firewalls, servers and sign-in systems to one platform, where analysts are alerted to unusual activity and can reconstruct an incident afterward. Which mitigation technique is the company applying?
explanation: Monitoring gathers logs and events in one place so that unusual activity is noticed and an incident can be reconstructed afterward. It observes and records but does not block anything by itself. Access control decides who may use a resource, segmentation divides a network into zones with controlled traffic between them, and isolation cuts one system off from the rest, usually to contain an incident.

question: A new branch router is put into service with the settings it shipped with. A week later an attacker signs in to its management page at the first attempt, using details from the vendor's public manual. Which hardening step would have prevented this?
options: Sending its logs to a central server
explanation: A device that keeps its factory-set account can be opened by anyone who looks up the vendor's default user name and password, so changing them is the first step in hardening a router. New firmware closes software flaws, encrypted management sessions stop a password from being read in transit, and central logging records the sign-in. None of these stops a correct password from working.

question: A patient notices that a hospital's online portal lists a penicillin allergy they do not have, and asks the hospital to amend the entry. Which privacy right is the patient using?
explanation: Data correction, called rectification in the GDPR, lets a person have inaccurate personal data about them fixed. Opting out stops a kind of processing, such as a sale of data or marketing, processing restriction keeps data but stops it from being used, and erasure, the right to be forgotten, has data deleted rather than fixed.

question: A penetration test report tags a finding as CWE-89. What does that label tell the developers?
options: The framework control that the finding violates
The finding's severity on a scale from 0 to 10
The type of coding weakness that led to the finding
The identifier of one publicly disclosed vulnerability
explanation: CWE, the Common Weakness Enumeration, catalogs types of software and hardware weakness, and CWE-89 is SQL injection: building SQL queries from input without neutralizing the special characters in it. It tells developers what kind of mistake to fix, and to look for elsewhere in the code. Severity on a 0 to 10 scale comes from CVSS, the identifier of one publicly disclosed flaw is a CVE ID, and a control that a finding violates comes from a framework such as NIST SP 800-53.

question: An authenticated scan of a hardened web server reports 14 critical findings. The analyst confirms that three of them concern services that are not installed on the server. How should the analyst treat those three findings?
options: As true positives, escalated and patched
As false positives, documented and excluded
As false negatives, rescanned and reviewed
explanation: A false positive is a reported vulnerability that does not exist on the target, so the analyst records why it is not real, keeps it out of the remediation queue and may tune the scanner to stop it recurring. A false negative is a real flaw that the scan missed, a true positive is a real flaw to escalate for patching, and an exception is a real flaw whose risk the owner formally accepts.

question: A server encrypts its disks and its backups and uses TLS for every network connection. Which copy of a customer record is still in plaintext?
options: The copy written to the database file
The copy saved in the nightly backup
The copy loaded into the application's memory
The copy sent to the reporting server
explanation: Data in use sits in memory in plaintext, because ordinary encryption must be removed before a processor can work on the data. Disk encryption protects the database file and the backup, which are data at rest, and TLS protects the copy crossing the network, which is data in transit, so data in use is the hardest of the three states to protect.

question: A worm spreads from one workstation to the next by exploiting a flaw in a file-sharing service. The vendor had published a corrected version of the service two months before the outbreak. Which mitigation technique would have removed the weakness the worm depends on?
explanation: Patching installs the vendor's corrected code, so the flaw that an attack depends on is no longer present. Segmentation would have slowed the worm by limiting which machines could reach each other, isolation would have contained each infected workstation, and monitoring would have revealed the outbreak sooner. All three leave the flaw itself in place.

question: One workstation renames thousands of files on a shared drive to a new extension within minutes, and staff can no longer open them. Just before, a process on it deleted the Windows volume shadow copies. Which type of malware do these indicators point to?
explanation: Ransomware encrypts files so that they can no longer be opened, often after deleting the volume shadow copies that could restore them. Mass renaming of files to one new extension is another common sign. A virus attaches its code to other files and spreads when they are run, a worm copies itself across a network on its own, and a rootkit hides malware from the operating system instead of locking data away.

question: A software company's most valuable records are its source code, its product designs and the algorithms that its engineers wrote. Which data type describes these records?
explanation: Intellectual property is the product of creative or inventive work, such as source code, designs and algorithms, and it is often an organization's main competitive asset. Financial information covers accounts and payment records, legal information covers contracts and court documents, and regulated data is data that a law or standard obliges the organization to protect, such as health records.

question: A company wants an AI model to lock user accounts it judges to be compromised, and auditors require a record of why each account was locked. Which approach BEST meets that requirement?
options: Keep the model's design secret so attackers cannot learn to avoid it
Use a model that reports the signals behind each decision
Pick the most accurate model available and publish its accuracy each quarter
Log each lockout decision with the account name, date and time
explanation: An explainable approach records which signals drove each decision, such as a sign-in from an unfamiliar country or a sudden change in behavior, so a reviewer can check and justify every lockout. An accuracy rate describes the model overall, not why it acted on one account, a log of who was locked out and when leaves the reason unknown, and secrecy works against the explanations auditors need.

question: Every quarter, the awareness team compares course completion, phishing click rates and the number of suspicious emails reported with earlier quarters, and presents the trend to leadership. Which part of program management is this?
explanation: Recurring reporting and monitoring tracks the same measures at regular intervals and compares them over time to show whether the awareness program is working. Initial reporting records the first baseline at launch, development is the writing of the training content, and execution is the delivery of that training to staff.

question: A threat profile states that a group has a budget of several million dollars a year and can afford to hire specialists and rent its own servers. Which attribute of a threat actor does the profile describe?
explanation: Resources and funding describe the money, people and equipment that a threat actor can put behind an attack. Level of capability describes skill, that is, how advanced the actor's own techniques are. Internal or external describes whether the actor already holds authorized access, and motive and intent describe why the actor attacks.

question: A clinic planned a web portal where patients would upload photos of their prescriptions. After weighing the privacy risk, it cancels the project before any development begins. Which risk management strategy has the clinic chosen?
explanation: Avoidance ends the activity that creates a risk, for example by dropping a project before it is built, so the risk is removed rather than reduced or shared. Acceptance would build the portal and live with the risk, transfer would shift the cost of a breach to an insurer or vendor, and mitigation would build it with controls such as encryption.

question: In a phishing simulation, 30 percent of employees clicked a link and typed their passwords into a fake sign-in page. Which mitigation addresses this behavior?
options: Locking accounts after repeated failed sign-ins
Requiring longer and more complex passwords
Training staff to spot and report suspicious email
Having each employee sign the acceptable use policy
explanation: Security awareness training teaches people to recognize phishing and to report it, which addresses the behavior that let a fake page collect their passwords. An acceptable use policy sets rules but does not teach anyone to spot a convincing fake, lockout stops repeated wrong guesses rather than a correct password, and longer passwords do not help when users type them into an attacker's page.

question: With each release, a vendor supplies a machine-readable list of the libraries and components inside its application, with their versions and suppliers. What is this list called?
explanation: A software bill of materials lists the components and libraries inside a product, with their versions and suppliers, so that a customer can check it against newly published vulnerabilities. A software license register records which products an organization is entitled to use, a configuration baseline records approved settings, and an application allowlist names the programs that are allowed to run.

question: Signed in with an ordinary customer account, someone calls the profile endpoint that every customer uses, changing the number in /api/users/1001/profile from 1001 up to 2847. Each request returns another customer's name, email address and phone number. Which flaw does this exploit?
options: No check on the internal addresses the server is told to fetch
No check that the record belongs to the caller
No check on which record fields a request can overwrite
No check of the caller's role on administrator functions
explanation: Insecure direct object reference, also called broken object level authorization, occurs when an API returns whatever record an identifier names without checking that the record belongs to the caller. A missing role check on administrator functions is broken function level authorization, unchecked writable fields are mass assignment, and fetching unchecked addresses on a client's behalf is server-side request forgery.

question: A large US retailer that sells online in every state receives a request from a California resident to see, correct and delete her personal information. Which law gives her these rights?
explanation: The California Consumer Privacy Act, as amended by the California Privacy Rights Act, gives California residents the rights to know, correct and delete the personal information that businesses meeting its size thresholds hold about them. GDPR protects people in the EU, GLBA governs financial institutions' customer information, and COPPA lets parents review and delete data collected from children under 13.

question: For several weeks, someone copied a company's source code through a contractor's valid account. Every login came from a hosting provider abroad, and the contractor's laptop was found to carry password-stealing malware. Which explanation do these facts BEST support?
options: An outsider exploiting a software flaw
An employee using the contractor's login
explanation: An attacker who signs in with stolen credentials is an external actor, even when the account belongs to an insider. Password-stealing malware on the contractor's laptop and logins from a foreign hosting provider point to theft, not to the contractor misusing granted access or to an employee borrowing the login. A software flaw was not needed, since every session used a valid account.

question: A flaw is found in the code on a server's motherboard chip that starts the hardware before the operating system loads. An implant that abuses it survives a reinstall of the operating system and a replacement disk. At which layer does this vulnerability lie?
explanation: Firmware is the code stored on a device's own chips that starts the hardware, so a flaw there sits below the operating system and survives a reinstall or a new disk. An operating system flaw would be removed by a clean installation with current patches. A hypervisor is the layer that runs virtual machines, and an application flaw lives in a program installed on top of the operating system.

question: A security team wants an alert whenever a cloud access token or private key turns up anywhere in the company's source code, including old commits in any of its 200 projects, so it can revoke the credential quickly. Which control fits?
options: Code signing of each release build
A web application firewall in front of the app
Static code analysis for injection flaws
explanation: Secrets scanning searches code and its history for credentials such as tokens, keys and passwords, and raises an alert so they can be revoked and rotated; many platforms can also block a push that contains one. Code signing proves who published a build, static code analysis looks for coding flaws such as injection, and a WAF filters web requests to a running application; none of them looks for leaked credentials.

question: A monitoring tool shows one workstation sending connection attempts to every TCP port, from 1 to 65,535, on each host in its subnet. Which activity does this pattern indicate?
explanation: A sweep of every port on every host is reconnaissance: the source is mapping which hosts and services exist before it attacks them. Data exfiltration appears as large transfers to an outside address. Lateral movement appears as logons or remote sessions from one internal host to another. A denial of service appears as a flood aimed at one target to exhaust it.

question: To save bandwidth, a company enables split tunneling on its remote access VPN. Which security trade-off does this change introduce?
options: Remote users lose access to their local printers.
Internal traffic travels outside the VPN tunnel.
Personal browsing adds load to the VPN gateway.
explanation: With split tunneling, only traffic for the corporate network uses the VPN, so the device's other internet traffic goes out directly and is not filtered or logged by corporate controls. Traffic for internal applications still travels inside the tunnel. Extra load on the VPN gateway and loss of access to local printers are drawbacks of a full tunnel, which sends everything through the corporate network.

question: Each year a bank's directors want an outside opinion on how well its security controls work. Which fact about a candidate audit firm would compromise its independence?
options: It was chosen by the board's audit committee
It audits several other companies in the same sector
It designed and set up the safeguards under review
It tests a sample of records instead of the full set
explanation: An auditor that reviews safeguards it designed and set up is checking its own work, a self-review conflict that destroys its independence. Auditing other companies in the same sector is normal, an external auditor is properly appointed by the board's audit committee, and testing a sample of records is standard audit practice.

question: Responders find that an intruder has controlled a domain controller and 23 servers for four months. What is the main risk of cleaning the servers one at a time over two weeks, rather than all at once?
options: Restored backups bring the implants back
The intruder notices the remediation and adapts
Memory evidence is lost in the rebuild
The intruder returns through the same entry point
explanation: A piecemeal cleanup warns a well-established intruder while they still control the systems not yet cleaned, so eradication of this kind is carried out in one coordinated action. Reinfection through an entry point left open, implants hidden in backups and the loss of evidence held in memory are real risks as well, but they apply just as much to a cleanup done all at once.

question: A financial institution requires every laptop to prove it has current patches, disk encryption and approved antivirus before it may join the wired or wireless LAN, and sends any laptop that fails to a remediation VLAN. Which solution enforces this?
explanation: Network access control checks a device's posture, such as patch level, encryption and antivirus status, when it tries to connect, and then admits it, blocks it or places it in a remediation VLAN. Port security limits which MAC addresses may use a switch port without checking a device's health, intrusion prevention blocks attacks in traffic, and patch management installs updates without controlling who may connect.

question: A web server log shows this value in a request: productID=5 UNION SELECT username, password, NULL, NULL FROM users-- The application places productID in a database query. Which attack is being attempted?
explanation: UNION SELECT and a table name after FROM are SQL syntax, so a parameter that carries them is a SQL injection attempt, here one that tries to add the user names and passwords in the users table to the page's results. LDAP injection carries directory filter characters such as parentheses and asterisks. Command injection carries a shell command after a separator such as a semicolon. XML injection carries added tags or entities.

question: Which of these records would a beverage company protect as a trade secret?
options: The published patent on its bottle design
The formula for its best-selling drink
The card numbers of its online customers
The legal advice it received on a lawsuit
explanation: A trade secret is business information, such as a formula or a process, whose value depends on its being kept from competitors. A patent is intellectual property that is published in return for legal protection, customers' card numbers are regulated data covered by PCI DSS, and a lawyer's advice is legal information, which is kept confidential under legal privilege and not for its commercial value.

question: An analyst presents a risk's annualized loss expectancy (ALE) to the board. What does that figure express?
options: The number of times a threat is expected to occur in a year
The loss a threat is expected to cause over one year
The maximum loss a single threat causes in any one year
The loss in dollars from one occurrence of a threat
explanation: The ALE is the loss a threat is expected to cause in a year on average, found by multiplying the single loss expectancy by the annualized rate of occurrence. Because it is an average, it is not the worst loss a year could bring, the loss from one occurrence is the single loss expectancy, and the expected number of occurrences a year is the annualized rate of occurrence.

question: Customers often type full card numbers into a support chatbot that sends conversations to an outside model provider and keeps them in logs. Which control BEST reduces the risk of data loss?
options: Redact card details in each message before it is sent out or logged
Warn customers in the chat window not to type card numbers
Sign a data protection agreement with the model provider
Keep chat logs for thirty days and restrict who can read them
explanation: Redacting sensitive data such as card numbers before it leaves the company or lands in a log means the provider, and anyone who reads the logs, never receives it: data loss prevention applied to AI prompts. An agreement with the provider still hands it every number, a warning does not stop customers typing them, and a short retention period still keeps them in logs for a month.

question: Which document states senior management's intent and direction for the whole security program and gives the program its authority?
explanation: The information security policy is management's high-level statement of intent and direction, and the standards, procedures and guidelines beneath it draw their authority from it. A physical security standard sets specific mandatory requirements, an onboarding procedure lists the steps for setting up a new account, and a remote access guideline offers optional advice.

question: Employees sign in once each morning to the corporate identity provider, then open the payroll, email and ticketing applications, which trust that provider, without entering credentials again. Which capability is this?
explanation: Single sign-on lets a user authenticate once to an identity provider and then reach many applications that trust it without entering credentials again. Passwordless sign-in replaces the password with a key or biometric rather than letting one sign-in cover many applications, multifactor sign-in asks for more than one factor, and a password vault stores and fills a separate password for each site.

question: A water utility's SCADA controllers run its pumps and valves. The vendor has released a firmware update that fixes a security flaw in the controllers. Which approach to this update is MOST appropriate?
options: Test it on the vendor's demonstration system
Test it on a replica of the plant
Test it on a virtual copy of the plant
Test it on the standby controller of each pair
explanation: An update for an industrial control system is tested first on a replica that uses the same controllers and logic but is isolated from the live plant, because a failed update can stop or damage a physical process. A virtual copy can model the process and logic but cannot run firmware built for the controllers' own hardware, and a vendor's demonstration system lacks the utility's own logic and settings. Updating the standby unit of each pair first is a way to install an update that has passed testing, but as a test it puts unproven firmware on live controllers.

question: After a data breach, the company's lawyers issue a legal hold that covers its backup tapes and email archives. What does the hold require the IT department to do?
options: Produce the data for the other side
Preserve the data in its present form
Log each person who handles the data
Notify the people named in the data
explanation: A legal hold obliges an organization to preserve every record that may be relevant to litigation or an investigation, suspending normal deletion until the hold is lifted. Producing data for the other side is a later step in e-discovery, logging each handler is the chain of custody, and notifying the people affected is a breach notification duty, not part of a hold.

question: A new rule says every customer record must store the country as a standard two-letter ISO code, and thousands of existing records must be corrected. The database team will run whatever update scripts it is given. Which role should own the corrections and confirm the records are right?
explanation: Data stewards look after data quality and definitions on the data owner's behalf, such as a field's permitted values and correcting records to match them. The custodian, here the database team, runs and protects the systems that store the data and carries out the changes it is given, a subprocessor is a third party that a processor engages, and the data subject is the person the data is about.

question: A company moves sign-in for all its applications from an internal directory to a cloud identity provider that users reach over the internet. Which attack can an outsider now aim at the sign-in service from anywhere?
explanation: An identity provider that is reachable from the internet invites password spraying, in which an attacker tries a few common passwords against many accounts from anywhere and stays under each account's lockout limit. Pass-the-hash needs password hashes taken from computers inside the network, shoulder surfing needs someone close enough to watch a user type, and a rogue access point needs someone within radio range. Multifactor authentication is the usual defense against spraying.

question: An attacker encrypts a clinic's file server and offers to send the decryption key in exchange for a payment in cryptocurrency. Which motivation does this demand MOST clearly show?
explanation: A demand for payment shows that the attacker's aim is financial gain, and the encryption is only the means of pressure. Service disruption as a motivation means that the outage itself is the goal, with nothing asked in return. Espionage depends on collecting information quietly, and revenge would follow from a grievance against the clinic, which nothing here suggests.

question: A SIEM rule raises hundreds of alerts a day for a scheduled maintenance task that runs on every workstation. The analyst has confirmed that the task is approved and harmless. What should the analyst do?
options: Escalate the alerts to the incident response team
Tune the rule to exclude the known task
Review and close each alert as it arrives
Quarantine the workstations running the task
explanation: Alert tuning changes a detection rule so that confirmed, harmless activity stops raising alerts while the rule still catches the behavior it was written for. Quarantine isolates hosts that are actually infected, escalation hands a confirmed attack to incident responders, and reviewing and closing alerts one at a time is how unclear alerts are validated when there are few of them.

question: A hospital portal already asks each user for a password. For a second factor, the security team wants one that is something you are. Which sign-in step meets this need?
options: Connecting from the hospital's own network
Scanning the user's fingerprint on a reader
Entering a code shown on a hardware token
explanation: Something you are is a trait of the user's body, so a fingerprint scan adds that factor to a password. A code from a hardware token is something you have, a stored security question is something you know and only repeats the password's factor type, and connecting from the hospital network is somewhere you are.

question: A company's asset inventory names one manager for each server. That manager approves requests for access to the server and is accountable for how it is used, while the infrastructure team patches it and backs it up. Which role does the manager hold?
explanation: The owner of an asset is the person accountable for it, who decides who may use it and how it must be handled. A custodian looks after the asset day to day on the owner's behalf, which is the part the infrastructure team plays by patching and backing up. An administrator carries out the technical work, and an auditor checks that the rules are followed.

question: A new accounts clerk is given access to the two file shares and the billing application that the job requires, and to nothing else. Which principle does this apply?
explanation: Least privilege gives each account only the access its job requires, so that a mistake or a stolen login can reach as little as possible. Separation of duties splits a sensitive task between people, a mandatory vacation makes staff step away so that others can spot irregular work, and defense in depth layers several controls so that one failure is not enough.

question: A PKI has an offline root CA and three intermediate CAs, one each for server, email and code signing certificates. The private key of the code signing intermediate is stolen. What must the company revoke to contain the theft?
options: The self-signed certificate of the root CA
The certificate of the code signing intermediate
The certificates of the three intermediate CAs
The code signing certificates issued to developers
explanation: Each intermediate CA limits the damage of its own compromise, because revoking its certificate invalidates everything issued beneath it and nothing else. Revoking the certificates already issued to developers leaves the stolen key able to sign new ones. The other intermediates use separate keys and remain trustworthy. The root CA is kept offline for this very case, so its certificate stays valid and can sign a replacement intermediate.

question: A SOC wants one tool that collects logs from firewalls, servers and cloud services, links related events from different sources and raises a single prioritized alert. Which tool fits this need?
explanation: A SIEM aggregates logs from many sources, normalizes them and correlates related events into prioritized alerts, which makes it the central tool for security monitoring. A SOAR platform runs automated response playbooks on alerts, an EDR platform records and responds to activity on endpoints, and a NetFlow collector gathers traffic records from routers and switches.

question: An employee turns off the screen lock on a work laptop because typing the PIN every time is a nuisance. In anomalous behavior recognition training, which kind of behavior is this?
explanation: Risky behavior is a deliberate choice that weakens security without any intent to cause harm, such as turning off a screen lock for convenience. Unexpected behavior is activity out of the ordinary, such as a sign-in from another country in the middle of the night, unintentional behavior is an honest mistake such as a misaddressed email, and malicious behavior is meant to cause harm.

question: A BIA finds that the order system loses $15,000 in sales for each hour it is down, must be running again within 2 hours of a failure, and takes 3 hours on average to restore. Which statement describes the gap?
options: The MTBF is below the vendor's stated rating
The MTTR is longer than the RTO allows
The backup interval exceeds the RPO
The ALE is above the risk threshold
explanation: When the MTTR, the average time to restore a system, is longer than the RTO, recovery will usually miss its target. Here a 3-hour average against a 2-hour RTO is that gap. A backup interval longer than the RPO would mean too much data loss, an MTBF below the vendor's rating would mean failures come too often, and an ALE above the threshold is a risk analysis finding rather than a recovery gap.

question: A router between a web server and a database server passes traffic from the web server's address to the database on TCP port 1433 and drops every other packet sent to the database. Which mitigation technique is the router applying?
explanation: On a router or firewall, an access control list is the set of rules that permits or denies packets according to their addresses, protocol and port. An application allow list names the programs that may run on a host, configuration enforcement keeps systems at an approved baseline, and port security limits which devices may connect to a switch port.

question: A playbook blocks at the firewall each address that appears in a threat intelligence feed. The feed lists a business partner's address by mistake, and the partner is cut off for six hours until someone notices. Which risk of automation does this show?
options: It adds complexity that makes the workflow hard to maintain
It acts on faulty input before a person has checked the action
It becomes a single point of failure for the security team
It builds up technical debt that is costly to remove later
explanation: Automation carries out its instructions at machine speed, so a wrong entry in its input is enforced before any person can question it. An allow list of partner addresses or an approval step for blocking actions reduces that risk. A single point of failure would mean that blocking stopped when the playbook itself failed. Technical debt and complexity are costs of building and maintaining automation, not of acting on bad data.

question: To meet a deadline, a marketing team pays for a cloud file-sharing service with a department credit card and stores customer lists there. The company's technology staff have not approved the service and do not know about it. Which threat actor type does this BEST describe?
explanation: Shadow IT is technology that staff set up and use without the knowledge or approval of the IT department, usually to get work done faster. It counts as a threat actor because data ends up on systems that nobody secures or monitors. A nation-state actor, a hacktivist and an unskilled attacker all set out to do harm, whether for a government's strategic aims, for a cause or with tools that others wrote.

question: A company replaces the MPLS circuits to its branch offices with SD-WAN over ordinary broadband and LTE links. Which security capability does SD-WAN add that the MPLS service did not provide?
options: Wireless encryption between branch laptops and access points
Encrypted overlay tunnels managed from a central controller
Private label-switched paths across a carrier's network
Per-device authentication before a switch port opens
explanation: SD-WAN builds encrypted tunnels, usually IPsec, over whatever links a branch has and applies routing and security policy to all of them from a central controller. Wireless encryption such as WPA3 protects only the link between a laptop and an access point, per-device port authentication is 802.1X, and private label-switched paths are what the MPLS service already provided.

question: A company wants its firewall to block Tor, which can use port 443 and resemble ordinary HTTPS, while still allowing normal web browsing. Which firewall capability makes this possible?
explanation: Application-layer filtering identifies the application inside a connection from the content and pattern of its traffic rather than from its port, so a next-generation firewall can block Tor while allowing other HTTPS. Stateful inspection only tracks whether packets belong to an allowed connection, port-based lists cannot tell two applications on port 443 apart, and MAC address filtering controls which devices may use a local segment.

question: A vulnerability's CVSS base score is 9.0. Which qualitative severity rating does CVSS give that score?
explanation: CVSS maps scores to ratings: 0.1 to 3.9 is Low, 4.0 to 6.9 Medium, 7.0 to 8.9 High and 9.0 to 10.0 Critical, so 9.0 is the lowest score rated Critical. High tops out at 8.9, Medium covers 4.0 to 6.9, and Low covers only scores below 4.0.

question: An earthquake destroys a company's main data center, and its hot site, in the same metropolitan area, is badly damaged as well. Which planning failure does this reveal?
options: Skipping regular failover tests of the hot site
Placing the hot site too close to the primary
Sizing the hot site for too little of the load
Replicating data to the hot site too rarely
explanation: Geographic dispersion keeps a recovery site far enough from the primary site that one earthquake, flood or storm cannot damage both. More frequent replication limits lost data, regular failover tests prove that the switch works, and sizing the hot site for the full load keeps it from being overwhelmed, but none of these helps when one event damages both sites.

question: A company sends simulated phishing emails to all staff every month and tracks who clicks and who reports each message. What is the PRIMARY purpose of these campaigns?
options: To test whether the mail filter blocks phishing
To train staff to spot and report phishing
To record that staff completed their required training
To see whether attackers could gain a foothold by email
explanation: Recurring phishing simulations exist to train staff to recognize phishing and report it, and to measure that skill over time. Testing the mail filter is a separate technical test, since simulations are normally let past the filter on purpose. Finding out whether an attacker could gain a foothold is the goal of a penetration test, and proof of course completion comes from the training records.

question: A company's public web store uses a certificate issued by the company's own internal CA, and customers' browsers show a certificate warning. What should the company do so that customers' browsers accept the site?
options: Enable OCSP stapling on the public web server
Replace the certificate with one from a public CA
Deploy the internal CA's root certificate using Group Policy
Switch the server to a self-signed certificate
explanation: Browsers accept a certificate without a warning only when it chains to a root already in their trust store, which for the general public means a certificate from a publicly trusted CA. A self-signed certificate chains to no trusted root, OCSP stapling only reports revocation status, and Group Policy reaches the company's own domain computers, not its customers' devices.

question: Two universities sign a document stating that they intend to share threat research with each other, while making clear that it creates no legally enforceable obligations. Which type of agreement is this?
explanation: A memorandum of understanding records an intent to work together without creating legally binding obligations, which suits an informal research partnership. A statement of work sets out the binding tasks and deliverables of a project, a service level agreement commits a provider to measurable service targets, and a non-disclosure agreement creates an enforceable duty to keep shared information confidential.

question: Training on anomalous behavior asks staff to report unexpected activity on their own accounts and devices. Which event should an employee report?
options: A notice at sign-in that the password expires in five days
A VPN message saying the session has expired overnight
A multifactor prompt to approve a sign-in they did not start
A lockout after they mistype their password three times
explanation: A multifactor prompt that the user did not trigger means someone else is trying to sign in with that user's password, so it should be reported rather than approved or ignored. A lockout caused by the user's own typing, a VPN session that expired overnight and a password expiry notice at sign-in are routine events with known, harmless causes.

question: A company's retention schedule says a former employee's records are due for destruction this week. The former employee wants them kept, unused, as evidence in a lawsuit. Which GDPR right covers this request?
options: The right to opt out of the sale of their data
The right to restriction of processing
explanation: Restriction of processing lets a person have their data kept but not used, and one of its grounds in the GDPR is that the controller no longer needs the data but the person needs it to establish, exercise or defend a legal claim. The right to be forgotten would erase the data, data portability gives the person a copy to take elsewhere, and opting out of sale is a right under laws such as California's, not the GDPR.

question: A company's routers and firewalls come from three vendors. Its investigators want every device to send flow records in one open, standardized format that can carry custom fields, so a single collector can store them for investigations. Which protocol fits?
explanation: IPFIX is the IETF's standard protocol for exporting flow records, developed from Cisco's NetFlow version 9. Devices describe the fields they send in templates, so devices from different vendors can export the fields they support, including custom ones, to one collector. NetFlow version 5 is Cisco's older format with a fixed set of fields, SNMP reads device status and counters rather than flows, and syslog carries log messages.

question: An order database has a recovery time objective of four hours and a recovery point objective of one hour. Which backup schedule meets the recovery point objective?
options: Full backups every night at midnight
Snapshots taken every day at noon
explanation: A recovery point objective of one hour means no more than an hour of data may be lost, so a copy must be taken at least hourly, and incremental backups every half hour meet that. Differential backups every four hours echo the four-hour recovery time objective but could lose four hours of orders, and nightly full backups or a daily snapshot at noon could lose most of a day.

question: A payroll clerk accepts a cash payment from a criminal group and, in return, installs the group's remote access tool on an accounting workstation. The clerk has no complaint against the employer. Which motivation BEST describes the clerk?
explanation: An insider who acts in return for payment is motivated by financial gain. Revenge would need a grievance against the employer, and the clerk has none. Service disruption would mean that the clerk wanted systems to fail, and political beliefs would mean that the clerk acted for a cause. Neither is suggested by a paid favor.

question: The vendor of a company's firewalls has ended support for the model, so newly found flaws in its firmware will not be fixed. The firewalls still work. Which mitigation technique removes this exposure instead of working around it?
explanation: Decommissioning retires a system that can no longer be kept secure and replaces it with a supported one, which is the only way to remove flaws that the vendor will not fix. Patching is not available once support has ended. Hardening the firewalls and monitoring them more closely would lower the risk for a time, but both work around flaws that would still be there.

question: Malware copies the authentication cookie from a user's browser, and the attacker reuses it after the user has logged out. The web application still accepts it. Which change would stop this reuse?
options: Requiring a second factor at each sign-in
Ending the session on the server at logout
Deleting the cookie from the browser at logout
Encrypting traffic to the application with TLS
explanation: Ending the session on the server at logout makes its token worthless, so a copied cookie cannot be replayed once the user signs out. Deleting the cookie in the browser leaves the attacker's copy valid, a second factor protects the sign-in that a stolen cookie skips, and TLS protects the cookie in transit but not from malware on the device.

question: A team describes its servers, networks and firewall rules in definition files kept in version control, and a pipeline builds each environment from those files. Which architecture approach is this?
explanation: Infrastructure as code defines servers, networks and security settings in files that are reviewed and versioned like software, so that every environment is built the same way and every change leaves a record. Software-defined networking programs traffic forwarding from a central controller, containerization packages an application with its dependencies, and serverless computing runs code without servers for the customer to manage.

question: An email's link text shows the address of the company's payroll site. Which check lets an employee see the address the link will actually open, without clicking it?
options: Reading the sender's full email address
Hovering the pointer over the link
explanation: Hovering the pointer over a link shows the real destination address, which in a phishing email often differs from the text on display. The sender's address reveals a lookalike sending domain, the message headers show which servers handled the message, and a padlock shows only that a page already opened uses an encrypted connection.

question: An analyst is building a timeline from a firewall that logs in UTC, a web server that logs in local time with a different date order, and a cloud service that logs in JSON. Before correlating the events, what should the analyst do while parsing them?
options: Drop the duplicate events within each source's log
Normalize each timestamp to one time zone and one format
Sort the merged events by the time each source recorded
Hash each log file to show it has not been altered
explanation: Parsing extracts fields such as time, source, user and action from each log and normalizes them, and converting every timestamp to one time zone and format lets events from different systems line up in the right order. Sorting by the times each source recorded mixes UTC with local time, hashing proves a file is unaltered but leaves its times as they are, and removing duplicates does not reconcile time zones.

question: Which control BEST reduces the risk that users jailbreak a company's public-facing chatbot into producing harmful content?
options: Redact personal data from each conversation before logging it
Screen both prompts and replies with a separate moderation model
Ground its answers in approved documents and cite each source
Use random session IDs and check who owns each conversation
explanation: Jailbreaks get past a model's own safeguards, so add a layer the model does not control: a separate moderation model that checks what goes in and, crucially, what comes out. Regular red-team testing finds new jailbreaks before attackers do. Grounding answers reduces hallucinations, redacting personal data limits data loss, and random session IDs prevent session hijacking, but none of them stops a model from being talked past its rules.

question: A coffee shop offers free Wi-Fi with no password and no encryption. Which threat can another customer on the same network MOST easily carry out against other users there?
explanation: On an open network with no encryption, anyone connected can capture and alter the traffic between other users and the internet, which is an on-path attack. Cross-site scripting and SQL injection exploit flaws in web applications from wherever the attacker is, and typosquatting relies on a misspelled domain, so none of them depends on sharing the network.

question: Every 15 minutes, a SOC's SIEM downloads an updated list of IP addresses, domains and file hashes tied to current attacks, and it raises an alert when any of them appear in the company's logs. What is the SIEM using?
explanation: A threat feed is a regularly updated stream of indicators, such as malicious IP addresses, domains and file hashes, that security tools can match against logs and traffic automatically. A vulnerability scan looks for weaknesses in the company's own systems, a CVE list identifies vulnerabilities rather than attackers' infrastructure, and a penetration test report describes what testers found at one point in time.

question: A user's browser suddenly fills the screen with a warning that the computer is infected and must be repaired by calling a toll-free number. The files are untouched, and the warning disappears when the browser is closed. Which type of attack is this?
explanation: Scareware frightens a user with a false warning, such as a fake infection alert, to push the user into calling the attacker, paying for a useless fix or allowing remote access. Ransomware actually encrypts or locks the user's files and demands payment to release them. Bloatware is unwanted software that comes installed on a device and wastes its resources. A logic bomb is hidden code that runs a harmful payload when a set condition is met.

question: A company keeps its production data on a server, a nightly backup on a NAS beside it, and a weekly backup on tape that is locked in a safe in the same room. What must it add to meet the 3-2-1 backup rule?
options: An offline copy of the data
A third copy of the data
explanation: The 3-2-1 rule calls for three copies of the data on two different types of media, with one copy kept offsite, so that a single fire or flood cannot destroy every copy. The company already has three copies on disk and on tape, and the tape in the safe is already an offline copy, but all three sit in the same room.

question: An auto-scaling group adds virtual machines whenever traffic peaks. Each new instance must start with the security agent already installed and forwarding its logs. Which approach achieves this?
options: Scanning each new instance for vulnerabilities at launch
Building the agent and its settings into the machine image
Signing the machine image and verifying it at each launch
Pushing the agent to new instances in a nightly job
explanation: A machine image that already contains the security agent and its settings gives every instance launched from it the same protection from the moment it starts. A nightly job suits long-lived servers but leaves a new instance unprotected until the job runs. Signing and verifying the image proves that it has not been altered, not that the agent is in it. Scanning at launch reports weaknesses and installs nothing.

question: Before a new accounts payable clerk starts approving payments, a security analyst spends an hour with the clerk alone, walking through the payment controls and the scams that target the role. Which delivery mechanism and type of training is this?
options: A learning management system; annual refresher training
explanation: A private session between a trainer and one person is one-to-one delivery, and training given to a new starter before they take on a role is initial, or onboarding, training. One-to-many delivery reaches a group at once, corrective training responds to someone's mistake, a self-service portal lets people find material on their own as part of ongoing learning, and a learning management system assigns and tracks courses such as annual refreshers rather than holding a live conversation.

question: A vendor releases a patch for a critical flaw in a company's ERP system, and attackers are already exploiting the flaw elsewhere. The patch has not been tested in the company's environment. Which fact about the ERP system increases the risk of delaying deployment until testing is complete?
options: It failed after an earlier vendor patch
It is reachable from the internet
Its patches cannot be removed once applied
It sits idle outside business hours
explanation: Delay is most dangerous when attackers can reach the vulnerable system, so exposure to the internet raises the risk of waiting for test results. An earlier failed patch and a patch that cannot be removed both raise the risk of deploying without tests, which argues for delay. Idle hours affect when the patch could be installed, not how likely an attack is.

question: A payment company's policy says that when a server that stored cardholder data is retired, its drives must be destroyed rather than wiped and reused elsewhere. Which risk does this policy address?
options: Recovery of residual data from the disks
Theft of cardholder data from live servers
Spread of an intrusion between zones
explanation: Destroying the drives of retired systems prevents residual data, which can often be recovered after deletion or an imperfect wipe, from being read by whoever uses the hardware next. Data on servers still in service is protected by encryption and access control, unpatched software by patching, and the spread of an intrusion between zones by segmentation.

question: A password storage function such as PBKDF2 repeats its internal hash operation many thousands of times before it produces the value that is stored. What does this repetition achieve?
options: It ties each stored value to a separate secret.
It raises the cost of each guess at the passwords.
It lowers the risk of two inputs sharing a hash.
It gives identical passwords different stored values.
explanation: Key stretching repeats a hash many times so that every guess costs an attacker real computing time, which slows brute-force and dictionary attacks on stolen hashes. Different stored values for identical passwords come from a salt, a lower risk of two inputs sharing a hash comes from a longer digest, and a tie to a separate secret comes from a pepper or a keyed hash.

question: Accounts of departing employees were staying active for weeks. The company now runs an automated job that disables each account on the day HR records the termination. Which control type is the automated job?
explanation: A preventive control acts before an incident to stop it, and disabling an account on the day employment ends removes access that a former employee could misuse. A detective control would only report accounts that are still active, a deterrent control discourages misuse without blocking it, and a directive control states the rule, such as a policy that accounts must be disabled promptly.

question: Endpoint telemetry shows svchost.exe running from C:\Users\Public instead of C:\Windows\System32. What does this finding MOST likely indicate?
options: A file posing as a system process
A rootkit concealing a system process
A macro launching a system process
Code injected into a system process
explanation: Windows keeps the genuine svchost.exe in its own system folders, so a process with that name running from a folder any user can write to is malware borrowing a trusted name, a technique called masquerading. Injected code would run inside the genuine process and leave its path unchanged. A rootkit would keep the process out of the listing altogether, and a macro that starts a system tool would start the real one from its normal folder.

question: A scan of an internet-facing VPN concentrator shows firmware from 2019 with several published CVEs. The vendor still supports the model and has released corrected firmware, but it was never installed. Which attack surface does this finding describe?
explanation: Software that has a published flaw and an available fix that nobody has applied is vulnerable software, and an internet-facing appliance in that state is an easy target. An unsupported system is one whose vendor no longer issues fixes, which is not the case here. Default credentials are factory passwords left unchanged. Open service ports are listening services that need not be reachable.

question: In a company's PKI, the root CA signs only the certificates of three intermediate CAs, which issue every user and server certificate. Between signings, the root CA stays powered off in a locked room. Which outcome is this isolation meant to prevent?
options: An attacker uses a certificate after it is revoked.
An attacker creates a trusted certificate at will.
An employee loses the sole copy of a decryption key.
An applicant is approved under a false identity.
explanation: A root CA is kept offline to protect its private key, because anyone who steals that key can create certificates that every device in the organization trusts. Use of a revoked certificate is stopped by CRL or OCSP checks, approval under a false identity is what a registration authority's vetting prevents, and the loss of a sole decryption key is covered by key escrow.

question: A security review finds that an online store keeps customers' card numbers in plaintext in its database. The store must read the full numbers again to bill repeat orders. Which change BEST protects the stored numbers under PCI DSS?
options: Hash the numbers and store the digests in their place
Encrypt the numbers and restrict access to the keys
Mask the numbers and log each time one is shown
Isolate the numbers and filter traffic to their segment
explanation: PCI DSS requires stored card numbers to be unreadable, and strong encryption with tightly controlled keys is a method that still lets an authorized system recover them. A hash cannot be reversed, so the store could not bill repeat orders. Masking changes what is displayed and leaves the stored plaintext as it is, and isolating the numbers on their own network segment narrows who can reach them without making them unreadable.

question: At a bank, a wire transfer entered by one employee must be approved by a different employee before it is sent. Which risk does this rule mainly address?
options: An insider completing a fraudulent payment
A clerk keeping rights from a past role
Malware moving from office PCs to payment servers
explanation: Separation of duties splits a sensitive task between people, so that fraud by one insider needs a second person to collude and an honest mistake gets a second look. Segmentation keeps malware on office computers away from payment systems, encryption stops an outsider from reading intercepted transfer details, and periodic access reviews remove rights left over from a past role.

question: A hospital's imaging workstations run an operating system that its vendor retired two years ago, and the vendor publishes no further security fixes for it. Which attack surface do these workstations represent?
explanation: An unsupported system is one whose vendor has ended support, so every flaw found from then on stays open for good. Default credentials are factory passwords that were never changed. An unsecure wired network lets someone plug in and reach other machines unchecked. A supply chain weakness arrives through a provider of hardware, software or services.

question: An attacker releases a worm that erases the disks of every computer it reaches. The attacker has no tie to any of the victims, makes no demand and states no cause. Which motivation BEST fits this attack?
explanation: Chaos is the motivation of an attacker who wants to cause damage for its own sake, with nothing asked for and no message sent. Financial gain would bring a demand for payment, and political beliefs would bring a statement of the cause. Revenge needs a grievance against a particular victim, which an attacker with no tie to the victims does not have. SY0-701 names this motive disruption or chaos, and SY0-801 names it fear or chaos.

question: An IT director wants one web page, kept current by the monitoring tools, that shows at a glance how many laptops are missing patches, which backups failed overnight and which certificates expire this month. What should the team build?
explanation: A dashboard pulls key measures from monitoring tools into one continuously updated view, tailored to its audience, so problems stand out at a glance. A runbook gives step-by-step instructions for a task, a packet capture records raw network traffic, and a syslog server collects log messages without summarizing them.

question: During a server room inspection, a technician finds a small unlabeled adapter connected between a server's keyboard cable and its USB port. Nobody on the team installed it. What is this device MOST likely to be?
explanation: A hardware keylogger sits in line between a keyboard and the computer and records every keystroke, and security software on the computer cannot see it. Finding one is evidence of a physical attack. An RFID cloner copies the data on an access badge, a card skimmer reads payment cards at a terminal, and a network tap copies traffic from a network cable. None of those connects to a keyboard.

question: A bank's web log shows a funds transfer request sent from a customer's own browser with a valid session cookie, but its Referer header names an unrelated forum. The customer says the only thing done at that moment was opening a post on that forum. Which attack does this indicate?
explanation: Cross-site request forgery makes a signed-in user's own browser send a request the user never intended, and the browser attaches the valid session cookie by itself. The request therefore looks genuine except that it began on another site. Server-side request forgery makes the server fetch an address the attacker chooses. A replay resends a captured request or token from the attacker's machine, and session fixation forces a known session identifier on the user before sign-in.

question: Two identical web servers run as an active-active cluster, and one of them fails. What happens to the traffic it was serving?
options: It resumes once a spare is built from backup
The remaining node absorbs it on top of its own load
An idle standby node is promoted to take it over
It moves to the DR site once failover is declared
explanation: In an active-active cluster every node serves traffic at the same time, so when one fails the others absorb its share without waiting for anything to start. Promoting an idle standby describes an active-passive cluster, resuming once a spare is built from backup describes a cold spare, and moving to a DR site after failover is declared describes site-level recovery.

question: A document that applies to every system requires passwords of at least 14 characters and locks an account after five failed sign-in attempts. Which type of document is this?
explanation: A standard sets specific, mandatory requirements, such as a minimum password length and a lockout limit, that support a broader policy. A policy states management's intent without exact values, a procedure gives the steps for applying a setting, and a guideline offers advice that staff may choose not to follow.
